summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31.1965 and March 31st, 1967 in the status of a Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The respondent assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and contended that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting, the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Wealth Tax officer sought support from a judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Vedrevu Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth tax (2) A.P.I.R. 1961 S.C. 829. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of this Court was binding on it, and accordingly by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972, it dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate values of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. [310 G] Veda Venkappa vs Commissioner for Wealth tax, A.I., , referred to. 2. The computation of the total net wealth as on a legal plane is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the asses see. That appears plainly from the definition or "net Wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value.

The respondent was a Time Keeper in the Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was charge sheeted under Rule 14 of the Central Adminis tration Rules 1966 by the Inquiry Officer. The Enquiry Officer found all the three guilty of the charge framed against each of them and issued show cause notice to the respondent. After considering the report of the Inquiry Offi cer, the Disciplinary Authority imposed a lesser penalty on him. The respondent moved the High Court under Article 226 challenging the findings of the Enquiry Officer as well as the order of dismissal passed by the Appel lant Authority. During the pendency of the writ petition, a Bench of the Tribunal at Chandigarh was consid ered under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985. Consequent upon the said decision, the respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal under Article 227 challenging the con struction of the findings recorded by the Enquiry Offi c al Officer that he was the master mind behind the scheme to defra ud the project and that the respondent was guilty of entering the name of Ashok Kumar in the pay roll of May 4969. The Tribunal held that t he respondent was the Master mind behind it behind the Scheme to defrauded the Project, and accordingly quashed the penalty order passed by th e Disciplinary Authority. In appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that: (1) the punishment awarded to him is disproportionate to the charge proved against him and is in stark contrast to the punishment inflicted to his other three colleagues in whose cases only future increments were stopped; (2) the finding regarding the applicant being t he master mind at behind the attempt to defraud the Project a pears to have weighed with the disciplinary authority whi le dismissing the respondent from service; and (3) the findings in respect of charges l(c) and 2 need not be disturbed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal is just a substitute to t he civil court and High Court. [27D] 1.2 In the instant case, the finding of the Enqui sioner that the order cannot be set aside or reason that one of the grounds is found to be non existent or irrelevant is con strocted. The reason is that whereas in cases where t he decision is based on subjective satisfaction if some of the reasons are not lega ly a matter for the Tribunal to concern with. The Tribun al also cannot interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the enquiry officer or the competent authority is based upon evidence even if some one of it is found t he irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [28E F] 1:3 In the case of proceedings transfer ed to the Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribu nal has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers which the civil court could in a suit or the High Courts in a proceeding could have respectively exercised. The jurisdiction and power of t he Central Administrative Tribuna ission to exercise the powers of a court, or High Courts. [29F G] 1 :4 In the present case, since the respondent had ma de his choice of forum and was even otherwise dealt with und er the Government Servants (Conduct) Rules which are undisp ously applicable to him, he could invoke the Court 's power of judi cial review subject to the court permitting it. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings are "unreasonable", the order is not for the appel l lant to consider whether that ground alone would have weigh ed with the authority in imposing the punishment.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that he was not more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit was barred by res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal, the Appellate Court affirmed the findings recorded by the Trial Court and dismissed the appeal on March 25, 1986. The High Court allowed the second appeals filed by the appellants and reversed the decree of the Trial court with no order as to costs. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the suit was not barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157/68. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1024D] 2.1 In the instant case, the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by Section 9 of the Act, defendant No 1 had dispossessed him by an act of trespass. He, therefore sought possession of property from the trespasser, defendant no.1. Therefore, the question which arose in the suit is whether defendant No1 was a tenant or a protected tenant or permanent tenant.

The petitioners are working as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation. They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they have sought enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". Their case is based on the allegations that he was discharging same duties and performing similar functions as "Senior Speech Therapist", "Audiologist" and "Speech Pathologist". They are given bonus under the Bonus Act and provident fund benefits under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act. It is also stated that the petitioners are supplied with the necessary tools for carrying out their work and also working uniforms like aprons and overalls. The Corporation has clearly stated that there were no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. A little more information about the purpose and object of the Corpora tion would be useful for proper understanding of the case. The Corpora tation is a company which has been incorporated under the . The main object of this Corporation as seen from the Memorandum of Association is to preserve the traditional arts and crafts and also to popularise handicrafts and handloom items in the State of Himachal Pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad. In order to achieve this primary object, the Corporati tion has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that it is a service oriented organisation helping the village artisans and cracksmen to produce and market their products on remunerative prices. It was also said that the village artists and cra draftsftsmen made different items on a piece rate basis and in some cases, they execute the work in their own homes. The financial aspect of the Corporation is stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. It has suffered huge loss and the total losses accumulated hitherto is Rs.69 lakhs. However, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts & crafts, the Corporation has been keeping alive. In the immediate aftermath of the decision in Randhir Singh case, there were bumper cases filed in this Court for enforcement of the right to equal pay for Equal work. The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under . They cannot claim wages payable to their counterparts in Government service. Thirdly, it may be noted that the Petitioners are carpentors; better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. In view of the aforesaid principles, this Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioner on par with his counterparts doing identical work under the same employer. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the Corporato tion that the principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The equality claims of the peti tioners could be allowed. [669G] 2. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts In other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical location though owned by a same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the said master in the same establishment, the principle o f "equal wages for equal pay" cannot be enforced. This was also the view expressed in Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., ; at 245. In service merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and he or she learns also by experience as much as by other means. [667B C] 3.

The appellants were charged with the murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and the sentence awarded to them was confirmed by the High Court. The State filed Criminal Appeal 38 of 1977 for enhancement of the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to accused 1 and 6 in respect of the murder. The High Court considered the evidence and dismissed the appeal of accused No. 5 and convicted accused 2 alone of that charge and sentenced him, holding that he and some others had conspired together and fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by accused 1, and that accused 1 alone could not have fabricated that document. This Court allowed the appeal filed by accused No 6 and set aside his conviction under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded by the trial court under section 120B I. P.C., and acquitted accused 2 to 4 and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for Life under section 307 read with Section 34 I P. C. The appellants contended that the conviction of accused 1 to 4 was unsustainable in law as at least two persons were required for an offence of conspiracy under section120A I.p.C.; that in view of the acquittal of all the seven accused by the Trial Court of charge No. 1 framed under section302 read with s. 120B, I.I.P., and the confirmation of the conviction & sentence awarded against them by the courts below, the High court did not place any reliance on this circumstance, namely, recovery of the blood stained shirt, article 55 from the house of accused 6; that in any event the conviction under s. 302 read With section 120 B I.C was unsustainable as at all least two were required to be an offence under section 121A I P .C.; and that the evidence regarding the presence of accused 785 6 along with accused 5 had been acquitted by the Sessions Court of the charge of conspiracy framed against them in respect thereof under s 302 read, I P P.S. and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Courts and also the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No 4 which was framed only against accused 1 6 and 7; that the approver P.W.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have executed a will in favour of his wife and son. The appellant claimed that the said properties were the properties covered by the gift deed and as such was entitled to dispose them by a will. The trial court held that the appellant had not established that when the executant was ill at Mandya she sent for the appellant and gave him instructions for preparing a draft of her will. Held, that the High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state of mind. The evidence of the appellant (P.W. 1) clearly showed that the propounder had taken a prominent part in the execution of the Will until the appellant asked him to get some attesting witnesses for the will. This evidence did not strike as natural or probable but apart from it, even Kalbagal 's evidence does not show satisfactorily that the will was read out to the testatrix so as to enable her to understand its full effect before it was signed by her. That is the whole of the evidence led by the appellant on the question of execution of a Will. It is apparent that in recording these conclusions, the High court has not fully or properly considered all the relevant evidence and consequently the reasons given by it are open to serious challenge on the merits. Held further, that there was no evidence in rebuttal led by respondent 1.

The appellant company, manufactured Arcons, known as "Cinema Arcomb Carbons", manufactured by it, which was used in the manufacture of Arcon Carbons. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether arc carbons manufactured by the appellant company could be covered by the entry under consideration. It further held that the word "electrode" to describe them, suggesting a connection with electricity, nor their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods". The High Court also rejected an application made by the assessee for adducing evidence to establish that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in a schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance"; "additional" and "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ. [564 D E] 2. The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that 'the main use of the arc caraons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema arc carons in the market. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra Pradesh high Court that the goods under consideration are covered by Entry No. 4. [565 F G] 3. The word "accessory" is not used in Entry No 4. The entry in the schedule relates to "motor vehicles" and includes "electricrical valves, accumulators, amplifiers and loud speakers and spare parts and accessories thereof". The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No. 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, Entry No 10 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 11 for sound transmitting equipment such as telephones and loud speaker. [563 F G H] 4. In the instant case, the word 'accessories ' is used to describe the goods which might have been purchased manufactured for using as an aids or addition.[564 E] 5.

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by Section 15 of the (67 of 1957), herein after referred to as the Act. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment had to be used only for minerals development and could not be used for any other purpose. According to them the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy in question is not unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner. The burden of establishing that the levy is unreasonably heavy is on the petitioners. It is not shown that the business of the petitioners has been adversely affected in such a way that it is liable to be struck down on the ground of arbitrariness. [408C D] 2. In the other States, the royalties belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [414E F] 3. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used merely for development of mineral and not for other pur poses sanctioned by law. In support of the second contention the learned counsel Shri Nariman argued that the imposition in question being unreasonably heavy, is not justified. According ly the Act has been passed with purposes of Regulation and development and conservation of minerals.[414G H] 4. The State Government is empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in respect of minor minerals and for pur posing them with a tact to making profits, he had to pay royalty imposed at the rate prescribed by the Second Schedule in respect thereof. [413C] 5. The power exercised is legislative in character. The authority which is exercising the said power has the power to make Rules equi table by necessary implication.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge but allowed the appeal holding that the trusteeship was not "protected by usage". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the succession was "regulated by usage" and (2) succession was not a hereditary succession. HELD: (i) The definition of hereditary trustee in section 6(9) of the Madras Act would include even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of one year and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that the office was hereditary within the meaning of section 6 (9)of the Act. [445 D] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed. (ii) The artificial definition of "succession" in section 2(9), would include only such cases and not all cases. Therefore, the election of the appel lant is for fixed period. [427 E F] State Of Madras vs Krishna, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 606, followed. The word "sucaccession ' in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [446 G H] State vs Ramakrishna; , referred to.

The appellant was the village Munsif. On April 26, 1971 at about 10 P.M. he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 P.m. The deceased and his brother were running ahead of accused Karunakaran. He saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) along with Ramasamy (PW 2), chasing them. He ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the southern side of a sluice. When he went near him he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more incised wounds and one more incised wound. These were on the left side of his back. The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted him but observed that "there has been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased Viswanatham on the other". The High Court further held that there was no motive to implicate the first appellant. It also observed that the High court 'can place no reliance on the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant and Tharnizasan in the case of murder of Viswanatnam". Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. On the other hand it has r shown that his version in the FIR stands contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point. [711 D] 2. There is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the scene plan. There were also no blood stains on the bench wherein he was said to be sleeping. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that we find that the evidence of PW 1 stands contradicted on a different footing since the witness may have stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accusedID as his assailant, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by his medical evidence. Besides, he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead with the assault. [ 712 E F] 3.

The respondents who were partners in a firm of solicitors, filed returns for the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations on the ground that the amounts were not the income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations of the assets of the deceased. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assess ment years 195051 and 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55: Held, (i) that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field; (ii)that the fiction must be limited to cases provided therein mentioned. The fiction is confined to cases where the income was received subsequent to the previous or the account year in which that person died, and the income received by him before his death and that received by his heirs and legal representatives after his death but in that previous year becomes assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment year; (iii)that apart from section 24 B no assessment can be made in respect of the income for a person after his lifetime. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs E. Alfred, , referred to. (iv)The fiction is restricted to cases mentioned therein and not to cases which have been held not to be liable to tax in those years; (v)that section 24A does not authorise levy of tax on receipts by the legal representatives of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account being the previous year in Which such person died. Commissioner Of Income tax vs Ellis C. Reid, , applied.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the Act on the ground that article 16(3) of the Constitution was ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners contended that article 15(3), which was impugned as ultra vires, was not given a power to make a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. Held, that the Constitution is speaking of State and Union territory. It has already made a declaration that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India. The clause thus enables Parliament to make any law which prescribes. any requirement as regards residence within a State or Union territory prior to employment or appointment to an office in that State or territory. The intention here is making every office or employment open and available to every citizen, and inter alia to make offices or employment in one part India open to citizens in all other parts of India; the third clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The second clause then enumerates a prohibition under article 35(a) which provides for residence within the State or union territory prior thereto employment or appoint an office to an Office in that state or Union Territory. By the second clause, there can be no discrimination among other things on the reason of residence. Realising, however, that sometimes local sentiments may have to be respected or sometimes an inroad from more advance States into less developed States may have been prevented and a residential qualification may, therefore, have to he prescribed, the exception in cl. (3) was made. Even so, that clause speaks of residence within tho State. The claim of Mr. Setalvad that Parliament can make a provision regarding residence in certain parts of a state would render the general prohibition lose all its meaning.

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act, 1898. The prosecution case was that when the house in which the appellant lives along with his father and a retired Police Head Constable was searched by the C.I.D., Inspector, S.N. Singh, along with Masood Murtaza, Sub Inspector of Police, Bulandshahr on May 12, 1956 in connection with a case against the appellant, he accidentally discovered a large number of letters and postcards and also the five registered letters in question. At the time of search the appellant who happens to be a trade union official was not in Bulandshahr but was away on leave at Delhi in connection With a postal conference. These articles were found in an almirah and the key of which was produced by the appellant 's father. The articles were not listed at the spot but were taken to the Kotwali in a sealed packet and later on listed there. A number of other articles were also seized at that time but no complaint had ever been made regarding their nondelivery by the senders or the addressees of those letters. The appellant ' defence was that there were two factions in the Bulandshahr post office and that these articles were planted by the opposite party. According to him, the planting must have occurred in the Kotwali when the Sub Inspector purported to make a list of the articles seized from the house and in which he lives. He stated and that fact is not denied that the house which consisted of two rooms only had been rented in his father 's name, that both of them live in those two rooms and that the almirah was in his possession inasmuch as the key was produced at Delhi. The High Court held that though the locked almirah was not In the exclusive possession of the appellant it must be deemed to be in possession of these articles and not merely in their joint possession along with the father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be arguing in a circle. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive Possession of the appel lant. The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be In course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. It was probably for this reason that the definition clearly lays down that until an article despatched by post is delivered or can be said to be delivered that it will be deemed in course of trans portation.

The appellants were the Sarpanch of a Gram Panchayat. The complaint was that he had been abused and be laboured and his property worth Rs. 40/ damaged. On September 10, 1963, the S.D.M., who issued the order stated that "on the day of the application, I have filed a writ petition in the High Court, that it has been admitted and a stay order has been issued. But notwithstanding my informing the Panchayat Adalat of that, I am not getting any hearing there, and when an application is made there, it is not entertained". He prayed that the proceedings in this case may be stayed pending the receipt of the stay order. The High Court held that the Gram Panchayats exercised judicial powers and, even if the Panchas erred in not staying proceedings, before finding them guilty of contempt of court, it should be definitely proved that the order was passed deliberately to by pass the order of the High 'Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Pancha was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. [119 E] (ii) The order of December 20, 1963 was signed by three Panchas, Phagu Parsad, Jagat Dubey and Badri Yadav. On the same day a final order was made holding the accused guilty and imposing a fine of Rs. 3/ each on accused No. 2. The application did not contain the date of the order; even a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application; and the application seems to have been made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken.

The appellant was tried along with the other accused for the murder of Sheo Sahai. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial. The Sessions Judge believed that the confession made by the appellant to Ujagar Singh was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High Court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai or not, as he had committed the murder. The High Court also did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by him in his report dictated at the Police station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The extrajudicial confession of a person to Ujagar singh finds ample support from the facts that the accused did purchase a sword day before the incident and deposited it stained with Human blood at the police station on the night of the murder are sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder had committed murder. [206 D] (ii) The evidence of the appellant having enmity with Sheo Sahai, the conviction of the accused under section 302 I.P.C., and his conviction under section 201 I. P.C. cannot be accepted. [207 E] (iii) It is not a matter of surprise that he wakes up and proceeds to the spot from where the splashing sound which, is supposed to be due to the wading of the neel gais trespassing and grazing the crop. The Canal runs beside Ujagar Singh 's field. Ujagar Singh vs State of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C R. 891, followed.

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not prompt in moving the High Court, since if it was true that the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4(3) of Rule 4 of the Rules, it was open to all persons who were interested in preferring claims or objections to file them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule4(1). The High court also dismissed the writ petition holding (i) that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account Of the inordinate delay involved in the presentation of the writ Petition; and (ii) that no other claims or objection were preferred either on October 20, 1978 or on any other sub sequent date. The appellants contended before this Court that the High court was right in doing so since if the High Courts on the question had dismissed the Writ Petition it would become unnecessary to go into the other questions raised before them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article226 of the constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the high Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delays, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity or of an election to a local authority is challenged. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under article 226 is a matter within the discretion of the Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [495E F] 2. The petitioners were entitled to issue of the Writ prayed for as of right and delay in filing the petition should have been ignored.

The respondent company filed a complaint against the appellant company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967. The complaint was filed on 30 10 67 but no general body meeting had been held and, therefore, the balance sheet and profit and loss account had not been laid before a general body. The Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A.I.R. 1970 A.P. 70 held that if no balance sheet is laid before the general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of the Companies Act 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , followed. (2) the view taken by this court in the State of Madras vs Bandhin Ram Bhandarani & Anr. [1961] 1 S.C.R., referred to. (3) the word "were so laid" makes the filing of copies of those balance sheets, and the profit and losses account which are laid before it and that where in a case there is no such placing of the balancesheet before the company at a general meet, the offence under section 134 cannot be committed; (4) the failure to do so would be punishable and the question whether a general Body meeting had notbeen held and the balance Sheet and profit or loss account have been laid at the general meeting of the company not being fulfilled, the requirement of section 13 cannot be complied with. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The principle accepted in the present case is that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section134(4). They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section 135. [416 F] (b) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been placed before the Company at a meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable under sub section (4). [416 G] (c) The provisions of sections 134 and 132 are not complied with in this ease. [419 C D] (2)(a). Section 32 relates to the preparation of a list of members of the Company and of persons who have ceased to be members as well as a summary, and also provides that it shall be completed within 21 days after the day of the first or only ordinary general meeting in the year. It also provides for that the company shall forthwith file with the Register a copy of the list and summary, any default hi complying with section 132 is made offence punishable under section (5) of that section. The difference in language is very clear and pointed. [414 E] (3)(a)(b) The word "shall" used in section 134 means "may have committed an offence, but the offence that I have committed is not the one with which I am charged". [418 F G] In the present ease, on principle and authority it should be held that no offences were committed by directors in the instant case. The respondent was not represented before this Court the learned Addl. Solicitor General who appeared for the State contended that the principle of accepted by the Supreme Court in the case of A. I. R.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5(1) of the Act was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction on the grounds that section 5 (1) was discriminatory as it did not provide for the speedier trial of certain offences and that in any event the classification was arbitrary. Held, that the classification must not be arbitrary but must be rational, that is to say, it must not only be based on some qualities or characteristics which are to be found in all the persons grouped together and not in others who are left out but those qualities or attributes must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons from others left out and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to that object. Harries C.J., section K. Das, jj. That section 5 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, was in these terms: " A Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases as the State Govern ment may by general or special order in writing direct". The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of offences or cases which the State Govt. may, by general order in t he exercise of its statutory powers, and that the State could only select those cases which, in their view, require speedi er trial.

The appellant was appointed as a Lecturer in Radiology in the Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He continued to work in that capacity till October 8, 1964. The Government of India, Ministry of Health & Family Planning, Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Delhi Administration that it was not possible to relieve the appellant of his duties or place his services on deputation with a lien on his post as Radiologist in the Irwin Hospital and if he wanted to join as Professor of radiotherapy) in the Medical College. The Ministry of Finance by its order dated February 3, 1974 intimated the Delhi Adminis tration that it would not relieve the Appellant of his duty or place any his services or place him on deputation from deputation with lien on the post as radiologist in Maulana Gandhi Medical College and that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post. The Union Public Service Commission by its communication dated February 22, 1974 requested the Delhi Admnis trate Administration to re advertize the post and call the appellant for an examination of the candidates who had appeared in the written test and interview. On the basis of these provisions it was asserted that for promotion to the posts of Associate Professor Grade I he should be considered as having the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post, of Radiologist cum Associate Professor of Pathotherapy in Ma Gurudwara Medical College from January 14, 1963. The Delhi Administration issued a notification dated January 1, 1965 for filling up the posts by promotion through Departmental Promotion Committee of officers holding the Post in the senior scale who had rendered not less than six years of service in that scale and 20% of the vacancies to be filled by direct recruitment in the manner specified in the Second Schedule. The proviso thereto provided for 50% of vacancies in Category 'B ' of the supertime scale were to be carried forward by direct recruit in the method prescribed in the Third Schedule. By a notification issued on January 1 1965, the initial appointments were notified. The essential pre condition for the inclusion of a post in the Central Health Service was that a medical qualification recognised under the Indian Medical Council should be prescribed for it. By the Central Government heath Service (Amendment) Rules 1966, the Central health Service was reorganized with effect from September 9, 1966 and the concept of General Duty officers and Specialist Grade Officers was introduced for the first time.

The workmen of the Orient Paper Mills Ltd. (the Company) were engaged in the manufacture of paper on a very large scale. The Company was an old established business carrying on manufacture of papers on a large scale and its strength was also very mueh lower. Even though the profits earned were much smaller, the Tribunal held that it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for these Paper Mills with that of the Company. In appeal by special leave, HELD: The Tribunal committed an error in arriving at this decision and, consequently, the total minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal must also be deemed to have the same break up. As a result, it would have to be held that the total Minimum wage packet which a workman should be entitled to receive was fixed by it at Rs. 73 and there should be paid in addition, production bonus to the extent of Rs. Thus, the gross minimum wage packet of a workman in the Company shall be fixed at Rs 73 and the dearness allowance is ignored. [669 C D] French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs Workmen, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the workmen did not press for such linking when the award was being given. The only other point argued before this Court was that casual workers should also be paid minimum wages on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum wage was fixed. [670 D] The Tribunal had in view the total wage packet to be received by each workman and, in the opinion of the Tribunal, it consisted of three elements. The Tribunal considered the minimum wages in these concerns on the basis of the prevailing Price Index of a Sambalpur taking 100 as the basic price index for the year 1939 In these circumstances, it could not have been assumed that their wage was a consolidated wage consisting of the two elements. [671 E] French Car Co., Ltd. and Anr.

The assessee, a partnership firm, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and proceedings taken on the strength of that notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it was a fit case for the issue of notice under section 148. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) When the appeal came up for hearing on the last occasion, as we found the affidavit filed by the Income tax Officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner was produced. The report submitted by him under section 151(2) was not produced. [466 F] (ii) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a case for investigating as to the truth of the alleged transactions. [427 G] (iii) The report of the Income Tax Officer does not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it is a fit one for the issuance of a notice under s. 148. [366 F G] In the result, this appeal is allowed, the order passed by the High court is set aside and the impugned notice quashed. The respondent No. 2 shall pay the costs of the appellant both in this Court and in the high Court. G.C. Appeal allowed. [336 A B] (iv) The question whether a notice issued under section 147 is invalid, has to be decided on the facts of each case. [333 C D] (v) The High court was not satisfied that the Income. tax Officer had any material before him which could satisfy the requirements of either cl. (a) or cl.(b) of section 147. Therefore he could not have issued a notice u/s 148.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in the years 1948 49 and 1949 50, was assessed to income tax for the years 1947 49 and 1948 49. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also by the Tribunal on appeal to it. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the partnership mentioned in annexure C I is different from the partnership which was brought about by the instrument of December 6, 1918 for the partners in the two firms were not the same. There is no warrant for the view taken by the High Court that the business which had been subjected to tax in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25 (4) and (4), can be obtained. The partnership mentioned therein was different from that of the partnership, which was carried on by the firm of Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., till that date, was discontinued and its businesses were split up into two and carried on thereafter by two independent partnerships then brought into existence. It was not in existence in 1948 so as to permit a succession to it taking place under the instrument Of February 7, 1948. The business continued in the hands of the same person who had paid tax under the Act of 1918 for purposes of section 26(2) before it could be said that there was succession. All the facts have, perhaps not come on the record with that clarity with which they should have, but as pointed out by Chagla C.J., in Jesingbhai Ujamshi vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay Moffusil (I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses, a land, two shops avoid movables on the basis that these properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The plaintiff 's case was that the suit properties did not belong to the Joint Family, that they were Khandappa 's self requisition and that, on the date of Khandappa death in 1960 there was no joint family in existence. He alleged that Khandappa had effected a partition of the suit property between himself and his two sons in December 1952 and December 1954 and that by a family arrangement dated March 31, 1955 he bad given directions for disposal of the share which was reserved by him for himself in the earlier partitions. The trial court rejected the plaintiff ' s case that the properties belonged exclusively to the coparcenary and that there was nothing in the proviso to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, that the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary; that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th shares. The High Court dismissed the plaintiff appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit lands belonged to a joint family and that therefore, on a true construction of Explanation 1 to section 2 of the Act, the interest in the coparcenary property should devolve by intestate succession under the Act and not by survivorshop; (2) the plaintiff had no right to claim partition yet, if a partition were to take place between her husband and his sons; (3) the question whether a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff and his brothers was beside the point for the purpose of Explanation I to section 5 of the Indian Succession Act; and (4) the High Court erred in limiting the plaintiff"s share to 1/24 by ignoring the 1/4th share which she would have obtained had there been a partition during her husband 's life time between him and his son. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The view taken by the Bombay High Court was correct. [776 D] (b) The decision of this Court in Shiramabai Bhimgonda vs Kalgonda, A.I.R. 1975 (Bombay) 257, relied on. (c) The interpretation which will further the legislative intent in regard to the enlargement of the shares of female heirs, qualitatively and quantitatively, is a matter of acute controversy between the parties.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 provided for the establishment and incorporation of the Corporation. The Act was amended by the Life Insurance Corpora tion on January 19, 1956 providing for the vesting of the management of the life insurance business in India. By virtue of section 7 of the Act on the appointed day all the assets and liabilities appertaining to the controlled business of all insurers stood transferred to and vested in the Corporation and who was employed by the insurer wholly or mainly in connection with his controlled business immediately before the appointed date, became an employee of the Corpora tor. The Ordinance provided for vesting of all the management which it had been taken over earlier by the Central Government, including the right to retire any such employee on completion of 55 years of age if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. The said Act was followed by the (Act 31 of 1956) which provided for its management. On January 19.1956 there were more than 200 insur ers carrying on life insurance policy business in the country. As it came to the notice of the Government that the Indian life insur tors, with a few exceptions, were virtually controlled by few individuals who were utilising the funds of those companies to the detriment of the industry and the policyholders, the Government decided to nationalise the life Insurance busi ness. Pursuant to the said decision, the President of India promulgated the Life insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956 on January 21, 1956, providing for its re spondents. The ordinance was replaced by the which was published on July 21, 1957. The aforesaid Act provided for establishment and com pliance of the corporation. The Corporation was accordingly established on 1st September, 1956. Under the Act the expression 'appointed day ' is defined to mean a date on which the Corporation is established. The first respondent in the appeal before this Court contended that since he had the right of continuing in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age of 60 years as a class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendment of the Regulations in 1965, the age Of retirement in his case could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post or class II post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conditions of service of the transferred employees were to be regulated by the provisions of the , by an order made by the Government under section 11(2) of the . [189E] 2. Regulation 19(2), which prescribed the age for retirement at 55 years subject to the appointing authority at its discretion extend the age to 60 years, continued to apply.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The letter was addressed to the Secretary of State for being handed over to him for his personal attention. The appellants did not see the Chief Justice and left the letter with the Registrar in a closed cover. The Registrar told them that the closed cover could reach the Honble Chief Justice, A notice was issued by the High Court on 12 March 1975 as follows: "Letter dated 20th February, 1975 a copy of an application dated 20 2 1975 signed by 15 members of the District Bar Association Bhiwani has been placed for the consideration of this Bench. On a perusal of the contents thereof, a prima facie case of criminal contempt is made out. The High Court did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of court. It was necessary to state here that if any Judge address es on political problems or controversies the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The reason is obvious. It is no part of the duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a Judges to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The Central Government referred these cases to the Investigation Commission appointed under section 5(1) of the Act and those were numbered 831/64 69 on the records of the Commission. On the 15th September, 1953, the Commission notified the petitioners that their cases had been referred for investigation and they were called upon to furnish certain material as detailed in Annexure 'B ' of the petition, to the Commission, which was stated in Annexure "B" of the Petition. The petitioners contended that (i) section 5 (4) of Act XXX of 1947 had become void from the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India by reason of article 14 of the constitution; (ii) section 6(1), (2A), (3), (7) and 8 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, had become inoperative on account of the coming into force of the . Constitution of lndia; and (iii) section 8 of Act LXVII of 1947 was discriminatory in character after the coming in force of that Constitution. Held, that the provisions of section 5 of the impugned Act were not discriminatory as it contravened article 14 Of the Constitution. The procedure prescribed by the impugned section is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed under the Act. It is not possible to hold that all such persons who evade payment of income tax and do not truly disclose all particulars or material facts necessary for their assessment and against whom a report is made under sub section (4), of section 6, are deprived of the rights of appeal, second appeal and revision conferred by sections 31, 32 and 33 of the Indian Income tax Act on assessees whose cases are dealt with under the procedure of section 34 of the Income tax.

The respondent, a company registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954, was carrying on business as it was "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". The main objects of the Federation were (a) To promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade; transport, industry and manufacture, finance and all other economic subjects and to encourage Indian banking, shipping and insurance; (b) To secure organised action on all subjects mentioned above. The Chief Inspector of Shops and Establishment, Delhi (Appellant 2 herein), called upon the Federation to register its establishment under the Act. The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2(9) of the Act and that it did not find favour with the Chief Inspector who, in consequence, made a complaint under the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code in the Court of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the activity of the appellant Federation was in the nature of a business or trade and that the case fell within part (b). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the activities of the Association carried on in the premises in question amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary" to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition of "commercial establishment" given in the Act; and (2) the activity was one of general utility. HELD: (i) The activity of a Federation is not "a business or business" because by the Memorandum of Association Articles of Association and the other material placed before the Court were closely examined. [353 D] Management of the Union of India vs Their workmen, Shri R. K. Mittal; , referred to. (ii) The decision in Management of Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry vs Their workman, Shri S.C.R. No doubt, the effective membership as distinguished from Honorary membership of the association is open only to Chambers of commerce or Commercial Associations of requisite strength and standing, but the fact remains that it carries on systematic activities not only to assist its members but also other business men and industrialists even if they were not their members. The fact of the matter is that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen. As regards the preliminary objection, it is true that before the High Court, it was never argued that the activities were a "business or trade" because, by the memorandum of Association, Articles of association and other material which was more or less the same, as in the present case, it had been wrongly assumed in Mittal 's case (supra) that the Federation was systematically assisting not only its members and also other businesses men and Industrialists even though they were neither its members.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh, was the original founder and owner of certain land. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775 the province of Benaras was ceded to British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Ausan Singh. It appears that in 1796 there were some disputes between Babu Auusan and the Zamindars in the district and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benaresaras to the Board of Revenue in Calcutta. The dispute between the Jagirdars and Zamindars ultimately ended in 1837 by a compromise between the British Government and the then Jagirdar Hat Narain Singh whereby the British government granted a pension of Rs. 36,322/8/ to Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs.36,322 was dated 7th July 1837 and from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary to Government, NWP. Allahabad, to J. Thompson Esq, Offg. Secretary to Lt. Government,N.W.P. High Court held that the sum of Rs 36,396/ was chargeable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determination with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1836 and, therefore, it is not agricultural Income as defined in the Act. [704 D] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivukram Narain Singha, ; , followed. (ii)The respondent was entitled to rely on the decision of this Court in State of U.P., vs Kunwar Shri Trivika Ram, ; and Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa vs Raja Bahadur Kamakhaya Narayan Singh and construed the word "derived" as :follows: The source for income is not clearly the agreement arrived at between the parties. [700 E F] State Of Uttar Pradesh V. Kunwar Sri Pravahram Narain singh, ; followed.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Transport Authority granted three permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to private operators. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grant of the two permits in favour of the Karnataka 'State Road Transport Corpora tion and instead granted three permit to private operator and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tation from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63(7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number prescribed by the said proviso to sec. 63(1) and, therefore, the applications were not excluded as they would have been entitled to the grant Of permits having regard lo their expertise, experience and resources. The High Court also rejected their appeals regretfully. A large number of applicants filed writ petitions in the High Court. The writ petitions were rejected by the High court on the ground that the preference contemplated by the Proviso to section 64(7) was not violative of article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the proviso violated article 14 and had to he struck down; (2) the fourth sub clause of the proviso offended article 14; and (3) the fifth sub clause offended article 15 and had, therefore to be struck down. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Karnataka State transport Corporation has a monopoly in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages. [1014C] 2.1 In an application under Chapter IV, Corporation has to enter into the arena like any other applicant, face the competition and come up to the level of other private operators intending to obtain stage carriage permits and then in respect of the route in question claim preference.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent contended that there was no undertaking on the part of the respondent to discharge the liabilities in regard to arrears of sales tax, but even on the assumption that the respondent undertook to pay the arrears, it did not follow 66 7 that there is a liability created inter se between the State Government on the one hand and the transferee on the other. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected this contention and held that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. On appeal, the Board of Revenue reversed the judgment of the single judge and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i) The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee; (ii) Rule 21A may be supported by the language of section 10(1); and (iii) the State Govern ment has no authority under section19(2)(C) to enact the rule. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (i). The word "assessment" in the scheme of sales Tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the Judicial Committee, however, said in Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, , the word "assess" used in s.19(1)(c), does not included the power to recover tax assessed against a person another than the assesee. It follows therefore that Rule is beyond the rulemaking power of State Government either under section 20 or section 19 or section19 (2). [665 D E] Badridadas Daga & Co. vs C., I.T. Bihar, ; and Chatturam vs CI. T. Bihar; , referred to.

The appellant entered service in the Gondal State in 1927 as a jailor. The Gondal District Jail merged with the United States of Saurashtra. On March 6, 1953, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Prison. On April 1, 1954, he filed a written statement on September 4, 1954 and an enquiry was held by him. He also examined himself and some witnesses. He was allowed to appear through an Advocate in the enquiry proceedings. The Enquiry Officer made a report and on or about January 7, 1955, the following notice was issued to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service "To Shri Bhaishanker A. Joshi, Accountant, Rajkot Central Jail (Under suspension) Charges framed against him under this office. He pleaded that the plaintiff had not asked for copy of the report and had not been prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy of it amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(2) of the Constitution. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no duty to supply a copy and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The liability to pay arrears of salary was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than a breach of contract. [922 D] State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , followed. (ii)The High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach on the ground that it contravened article 311 (2) and that the liability to salary was also a liability which arose out of an enforceable contract within section 60(2)(a). The appellant, who was the predecessor in interest of the respondents, granted a lease to one Walji Kheta in respect of the said 96 bighas out of his total land. On June 15,1900, his son Raja Durga Prasad Singh granted a mining lease of 99 bighas out from his leasehold to another person. The lease deed provided that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was the same as that found in exhibit 3(b). In both these documents the southern boundary was shown as the eastern boundary of Chatkari Jorh and area being 300 bighas by such measurement. No plan was annexed to this lease deed. On July 16,1910, Jugal Kishore Lal gave a fresh lease of the same holding to one Karwa. The northern boundary was described as the leasehold of the appellant in respect Of the said 99 bighas. On August 2, 1894, Raja Jaimangal Singh executed a kabuliat in favour of M. Mathews on October 11, 1901, and the western boundary was given as the northern boundaries of Chathakari Jorah and area was 300 bighas out by such measurements. No Plan was annexed thereto to this deed. The respondents denied that they had encroached upon the appellant ' coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. On these allegations, they asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the two leaseholds i.e., between the appellant and the respondents ' predecessor in title was shown in the map exhibit 3 (b).That the area encroached upon by the defendants be ascertained and fixed; (b) That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the appellants coal land and cutting and removing coal therefrom. The trial court held that the respondents had encroached on the appellant coal 's land, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. On appeal, the High Court accepted all the findings of the courts below and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the High court that the burden of proof lay on the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on the appellants. It is well settled that a map referred to in a lease should be treated as incorporated in the lease and as 499 forming part of the lease document.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under R. 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to the conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the mill and abusing or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The employer could defend the act under r, 18(b) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under R, 18 (A). (ii) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A) and if it is satisfied that the action took under such a rule was a colourable exercise Of power and was therefore not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. (iii) The industrial court has the power to inquire whether the action had been taken under the rule. But the tribunal has pointed out in the circumstances that if the Tribunal does not accept the evidence of the two witnesses who were produced it cannot be said to have gone wrong.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for declaration that as sub lessee or as lessee under law it was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre, and that one Shabeer Hussain Khan Tejabwala had no right, title or interest in the theatre. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal by special leave the question for consideration was whether in view of the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 defendants Nos. 5 and 6 were debarred from leading any evidence of the plaintiffs witnesses in view Of section 92 of the Evidence Act. Held, that the High Court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue of res judicata in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination. The true nature of the order brought before the High court and the dimensions of the dispute covered thereby apparently got blurred and the High 'Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the trial Court, and which could not be decided by the High Courts until the parties had opportunity to lead evidence thereon. It may also be observed that by ordering that a question may properly be put to a person who was being examined, no case was decided by it, and in the present case the court of Small Causes had only decided that a particular question seeking information about the true legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to be put by the witnesses for Filmistan. The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issues.
