The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial", and compelling reason". [367E] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , referred to. (2) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of conviction merely because another view is also possible. [368C D] Sanwar Singh vs State o/P. & Anr., A.I.R. 1971 S.C. 460; and Khem Karan & Ors vs State Of U.P. and Anr. , referred tOccasionally phrases like 'manifestly illegal ', grossly unjust, have been used to describe the orders of acquittal which warrant interference. But such expressions have been employed more as flourishes of language, to emphasise the reluctance of the Appellate Court to interfere with an order of discharge than to curtail the power of the appellate court to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion, bearing in mind the considerations mentioned by the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup 's case. Occasionly phrases like `manifestsly illegal, grossly unfair ' have been use to describe them the orders passed of acquittal as sentences which warrant interfere. But, such expressions had been used more as a flourishes or of language to emphasise their reluctance of Appellate Court, to interfere in the interest of justice, lest the administration of justice be brought to ridicule. That is what the High Court has done in this case. [369E F] San wat Singh & Anr. vs The State of U. P., AI. R. 1971 SC 460; referred to and re affirmed those principles. After Sanwat singh vs State, A.l.R., 1971 S C. 460, approved. (3) An injury of the nature received by the deceased could have been caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [367G H] Sanawat Singh & ors. vs state of Rajasthan A.P., ; , followed.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was appointed under Article 124 and under Article 217 of the Constitution, he was given the power to appoint Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of the State. The President had not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge from his office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less than two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, had been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or inca pacity. The appellant contended before this Court that (i) the President was given power to appointment the Judges of a High Court; (ii) the power of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief justice, under clause (e) of sub section 1 of Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 is not applicable to the case of a judge of the high Court or of the Bombay High Court and (iii) the sanction thereunder can be obtained for the prosecution of a person holding such an office. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power to punish a Judge including Chief Justice, of the highest Court as also a Judge is a constitutional functionary appointed under article 124 and Article 217(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [219D E] 2. The Constitution, while dealing with such constitutional functionaries, contemplated merely their removal from office in the manner provided in Article 124(4) as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by the Parliament under Article124(5) of the Constitu tion, even for investiga tion and proof or any misbehaviour committed against a subordinate Judge instead or of general law is clearly visualized when the allegation of corruption against a senior Judge and a Special Law enacted by Parliament under article 123(5). [220E F] 3. The provisions of Article 124 are as follows: 217. "if he or any person on his behalf is in possession or has, at any time during the period of his office, been in possession for which the public servant cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income". If it is held that a member of the higher judiciary is not liable to prosecution for an offence under Section 5 on account of the requirement of previous sanction under Section 6, it will follow that he will be immune from the prosecution not only under section 5(1)(e) as is the present case but also for the other offences under Clauses (a) to (d). The difficulty of sanction under section 6 for the provi sions as enjoined by Section 6 of the Act is, therefore, of considerable importance to decide the main question in this appeal. [321F G] 4. The scheme of the Criminal Procedure Code is that a public servant who commits the offence of criminal misconduct, as defined in the seven clauses of Sub section (1) of Section S 5 can be punished in accordance with sub section (2) of section 5 after investigation of the offence in the way prescribed and with the previous sanction of the competent authority obtained under Section6 of the . [322G H] 5. The right to appoint a Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 2 18 read with article 124(5)(4) and (5) and placed before the President, a Judge cannot be removed from his post unless and order to that effect is passed by the President.

The appellant, a member of the Scheduled Caste, challenged the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his prayer to be declared elected. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent 's case was that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri caste and (ii) the appellant was a Sunri by caste but was excluded from the Scheduled Castes group because he belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunirs known as Sahas. HELD: (i)(a) The Tribunal came to its conclusion that it had not been prov ed in this case that the respondent belonged to the smaller caste groups of Sahas and did not, therefore, belong to the Scheduled caste specified in item 40. [391 D] (b) The expression "excluding" denoted that the Sahas contemplated would, but for this word have come within the Sunri castes, no question of Saha ' being a distinct class independent of Sunriscould arise. [392 E F] (c) The finding that Sahas were a caste group within the reserved category must be held to belong to that caste and not those within that caste who formed the smaller Caste group of Saha s. [393 G H] (d) The appellant was therefore a Suniti by caste and had not, been proved to belong lo the Scheduled Tribe specified in Item 40. That being so, the election petition must fail.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was alleged that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948, and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The prosecution case was that the appel lant demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 which was later on reduced to Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The appellant denied any aiding and abetting the prosecution and also abetted him in the commission of the two offences. The defence was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The Magistrate convicted him under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and sentenced him to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30, 000. The wife was acquitted by the Sessions Judge but the High Court summarily dismissed his appeal on 20 2 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the word "relinquishment" was not a term of art and was used in the section; (2) the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition of the relin quishment by a tenant of his tenancy and that in the present case there was no such relinquishment. HELD : Dismissing the appeal: (1)(a) The word "reinquishment ' does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the 55 424 relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. [422 D E] (b) The words "the relinquishment of his right of tenancy of any premises" do not occur In the Transfer Of Property Act, but it was found in several of the Acts in different provinces wherethere are Secs which deal With the 55 425 relinquishment of its holdings by tenant in favour o the landlordby notice given in writing to him. The section in question, it should be further noted, does not speak of relinquishment or giving up possession,in general terms.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership Firm. The partnership was dissolved and in 1974 the undertaking became one of the divisions of Tata Sons Limited. It functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and does not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306 were members of the Tata Engineering Employees Union. They served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1)(d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that the Efficiency Bar as a feature of the wages scale should be removed, and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the suggestion of the union that a flat increase to the pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. It also held that there would be a resultant increase in the dearness allowance, house rent allowance and house rent allowances. The Union appealed to this Court by special leave against the order of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of reference in the State Govern ment 's order required the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay and dearness allowances, and there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in basic pay of individual workman. The financial capacity, as the Tribunal observed, constituted one of "the principles which are required to be followed in the fixation of the Wage structure". A clear statement of its intention is found in paragraph 22 of the award where the Tribunal stated: "I only propose to modify the existing structures of the scales with flat increases in each category". The fitment has also to be done only after the flat increase is added to the present basic salary of each employee. [177 D E] 2. The amendment made by the Tribunal has the effect of providing a second increase, this time to each individual workmen. If, as a result of any flat or ad hoc increases of salary, the workmen were to be fitted into the revised scales of Pay, it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. In the case of several senior employees, the revised scale would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in size of the pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they, surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them That was why the Industrial Tribunal thought that an all round flat increase of Rs. 150/ in the case Of the category of Draughtsmen and Rs.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said award. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded did not amount to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant, to pay the respondents the prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. The authority rejected both the contentions and held that section 2(vi) included wages prescribed by it and rejected the appellant 's contention that the applications made by the res pondents were incompetent under section 15 of the Act before the Patna High Court, because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed in section 2 (vi). The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section 15 was applicable to the case, because, the wages prescribed were not included in the definition, is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by an award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the . [422 D E] (ii) The appellant ' s contention was not accepted by the authorities below.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged under section 409 with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which was under his charge. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. On appeal by the State to the High Court it was discovered that there was no order sanctioning the prosecution, and that sanction had not been obtained for the prosecution under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that sanction under section 198(1), of the Criminal Procedure Code, is necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409, and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The question whether sanction was necessary under section 196(1)(i) of Criminal P.C., must depend on the facts of each case. If the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties attached, then no sanction would be required. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The State of Bombay ([1952] L.R. 75 I.A. 185), approved. Shree kantiahRamayya Munimalli vs Emperor (1948) L. R. 75 1. A. 180, 1308 ing to the office as to be inseparable from them, then sanction under s 197(i) would be necessary; but if there was any necessary connection between them and the performance of those duties, the official status furnishing only the occasion or opportunity for the acts, then, no sanction is necessary. Shreekaantiah R. W. Mathams vs The King ([1948] L .R. 76 I. A 180), Albert West Meads vs The Queen ([1949] L,.R. 74 I.As. 185) and Alberts West Meadads vs State of We8t Bengal ([1951] L,R. 73 I.L. 75, referred to.

The assessee, a private limited company, filed its income tax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90,947 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (1) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State of Travancore. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State. On reference by the High Court, the High court answered the question in favour of the appellant. Held, that the words "profits or gains" used in section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, are not restricted to business in British India and the proviso is a modification of the method of computation under section 10(2) of that Act for (1)[1953] S.C.R. 279, followed. The mere use of the words loss of profits or gains to be set off against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. There it was held that section 10 Of the Indian Act had to be read with section 14(2)(e) and if profits could not be added for the purposes of total income " losses sustained also could not he deducted.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the Company was at Calcutta. It had branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appeared to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees for the age Of retirement. The first respondent claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he had completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the time of their retirement at 55 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years and it was not correct to say that the trend in Bombay regions had been correctly fixed by the Company. On appeal by the workmen, this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal has rightly held that no such trend is established in fact. [434 D] (ii) The question of age of retirement for the workmen of the respondent should be fixed at 60. [427 E] (iii) The first Respondent was an All India concern and that changing the terms and conditions of service in regard to the age, of retirement and hours of work and other similar matters industrial tribunals attach much weight to what has been done in other industrial concerns in the neighbourhood in recent time whether by agreement or by adjudication. [ 427 G] (iv) The second respondent was an all India concern. There is no indication at all as to how long ago the age was fixed at 55 or at 58.

The first respondent was appointed Managing Director of the company from December 5, 1961 and his appointment and remuneration were approved by the Central Government on July 30, 1962. T. T., [335 F] (iii) The provisions of sections 237(a) and 239(b), have been utilised by the appellant as a cloak for taking action under the provisions Of section 235.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court drew from this conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits, and convicted them accordingly under section 411 I.P.C. and sentenced them to five years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption under section 41 1 722 Indian Penal code or at the most under section 412 of the Code had not been stated by law and therefore it was necessary always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. HELD: The law advocated by this Court is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, it may be possible for them differ from case to case. [723 F] In the present case the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who was the dacoits.

[225G] 1.2 The provisions Of neither Section 2 nor Section 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by Article 14 of the Constitu tion. [226H; 227A B] 1:3 The provisions contained in neither Section 3 nor Section 4 nor Section 6 or Section 7 of the Act are hit either by any limitation limitation. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed. Rule nisi is discharged. No order as to costs. [227F G] 2.1 In view of the fact that the substance known as 'thinner ' as it was or mixing with some other substances, are taken as intoxicating spirit endangering the life. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale in that area. No question of discrimination can arise in such circumstances. It is in exercise of this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by the following Rule: "13 (1) All poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept by a chemist, druggist or compounder for the purchase of dispensing or compounding in compliance with the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner) shall be kept in a box, almirah, room or building in a separate closed receptacle of glass, metal or earthenware. Entries relating to interest were posted till the end of Samvat Year 2006 in the account on the amount due at the foot of the account. The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio Additional District and sessions judge of Mayurbhanj Keonjhar. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of the administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work continue in that post for an unduly long time. The Orissa Superior judicial Service (Junior Branch) is the combined cadre comprising of officers held purely judicial post as well and posts which were essentially administrative. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the Registrar of the High Court is exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor has any hand in his appointment. The power to transfer a district judge from one post to another whether as a Judge or to one of posts in the secretariat was that of Governor though that power was always exercised in consultation with the High court and by large on the recommendation of the State Government. In these circumstances, the High 'Court was within its powers in posting Shri B.K. Patro as district and Session judge of Ganjam Boudh division, Shri P.C. Dey as superintendent and Legal remembrancer and member sales tax tribunal respectively. The question for decision in that case was whether the Government of West Bengal was competent to institute disciplinary proceedings against an addl. District Judge and sessions Judge of Mayusturbhanj. The State Government by its letter of April 2, 1965 intimated that it had no objection to adhere to the principle of three years service in an appointment at a particular station against a special post. But when it came to the question of implementing that policy, the Government was reluctant.

The petitioner filed a suit for title and injunction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was a compromise between the father and his two sons, and that the other will was a forged one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the alienees that the alienations were for about a purported consideration of Rs. 4 lakhs. Dismissing the special leave petition, HELD: 1. The alienees have admittedly been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Admittedly, the transfers are pendente lite. In fact if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No. 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in favour of the petitioner. The alienation deeds indicate that a sum of Rs, 1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. [541E F] 2. The alienations are for about the purported consideration. of Rs 4 lakhs and the sale deeds indicate: that a certain sum of money had been paid earlier and the net amount payable under these transactions has been received before the registration authority. The transferees have admittedly not received the sum of RS. 1 lakh has not been able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [543F G] 3. The High Court was in error in holding that once the court was satisfied that there is a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court, to act otherwise. [542G H] 4. The sale deeds are subsequent to 21.8.1987. In view of this direction, the security furnished in the Trial Court shall stand discharged and the alienee will have no liability to account for mesne profits. [544F G; 543A B] 5.
