The workmen of the appellant company, who were working as a textile mill in Baroda, claimed that they had been granted sick leave for two days and claimed that the benefit under the scheme of the Act was much less than the normal earnings of an employee and was not beneficial to the workmen. The Industrial Tribunal held that the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of the , were admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969 and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that as the benefits under sections 47 & 49 of tile Act were already available to workmen, the Industrial Tribunal committed a error of fact in granting additional benefits to the employees and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain it. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has examined this aspect of the controversy also and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the case of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question were illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [83 D E] 2. The benefit of sick leave was therefore lost when the Act came into force in the region concerned on December 14. 1969 and it has not been disputed before us that till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave with wages for periods varying from 6 to 10 days.

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed against him on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and there was a sudden search by the police on the 24th August, 1954 at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor. which in fact was not found but it was found that the appellant was carrying on espionage on behalf of the Portuguese Government with the help of underground workers. The order of the detention was challenged on the following grounds: (1) The detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos; (2) The order was mala fide as it was passed for the ulterior purpose of preventing his freedom of speech and freedom of professional activity in the sphere of Goan affairs by reason of his known views in this behalf. Held, that the right to be furnished particulars under article 22(5) to enable a proper representation being made is subject to the limitation under article 21(6), whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The requirement for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to supply cannot be implied In these circumstances it is necessary to have an idea of the grounds of preventive detention as furnished. The necessity for such communication would arises only if a detenue feeling, feeling the ground to be precise, asks whether particulars which would enable him to make a representation against the order of his detention.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged under section 120B read with section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 5(1)(a) read with r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The trial court held that the conduct of the respondent was most unbecoming of an officer and ordered administrative action to be taken under r.14 of the said Rules. On appeal by the Union of India, the High Court held that r. 12 of the Rules, 1953, was ultra vires the . Held, that r, 14 of Army Rules 1954 is not ultra vires. Rule 14 of 'the Army Rules does not impose any restriction on the power conferred by section 191 of the . The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service. Rule 15(1) of the Defence of India Rules, 1955, does not confer any arbitrary or uncontrolled powers on the Central Govt. under section 19 of the read with rule 14 of that Rules. The words 'subject to . , the provisions Of this Act ' occurring in s.19 makes section 21 subject to the other provisions of the Act and such rules, the Central government may dismiss or remove from the serv ice any person subject to this Act. Rule 16(1), therefore, does confer arbitrary powers on a court martial.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti. The respondent filed an appeal before the Standing Committee under section 124(5) of the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958, before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni, which was rejected by its resolution dated April 6, 1964. Thereafter, the respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the resolution dated March 6, 1963 passed by the Standing committee. The High Court held that the octroi duty had been levied in accordance with law and that it could be imposed only on the goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule I item 1, and that the levy was good after the octroi limits were fixed on January 14, 1964; and that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The fixing of the octroi limit with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy of octroi duty. [216 E] (ii) Rule 3(b) does not require the Panchayat to fix the octroi rates in the resolution passed under r.3(a). The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [217 F] (iii) Rule 5 does not empower the Panchayat Raj Authority to fix octroi limits in the Resolution passed under rule 3(a), and this procedure is made applicable to the imposition of various taxes mentioned in the other parts of the Rules. Viewed in this background, it seems to us that r .3(b), which authorises the levy is r.22, but it enjoins that the procedure prescribed in rr.3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duties can start being levied, r.21 must be complied with.

The appellant was convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1)(XIV of the , and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250, and accused No. 1 to a penalty of Rs., 50, 736 The appellants contended that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the words " pendency of any conciliation proceedings ". Held, that the provisions of section 12(6) Of the , did not support this contention. Section 12 contemplates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within a fortnight and if proceedings were not closed but were carried on as they were in the present case or if the Conciliation Officer does not make his report within 14 days he may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) Of tile Act. The provisions of sub section (6) of section 20 apply to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the report of the Conciliation officer is received by the appropriate Government or when the reference of the Board is published under section 17, as the case may be. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the complaint under section 12 (6), is made by the Conciliation Offi cer but when that report is received after the appropriate Govern ment. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conciliation proceeding should be held to terminate when the Conciliation Officers is required under section12(6), and the termination would depend upon how soon a report is receive by the Government.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The order states that on 24.12.1985, between 10 and 10.30 A.M., the subject alongwith Ramashish Bangali, Gulam, Rambriksha armed with Rifle, gun etc came in Car No. BHG 9372 on Katras Coal Dump and started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish his criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers. The order stated that the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner under section3(2), of the Act, passed an order on 24th December, 1985, rejecting the representation of the detenu and also the appellant/petitioner was informed that the said representation was rejected. Thereafter, the petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed without any speaking order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principles applicable in these types of preventive detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 with W. P. (crl) No. 1265/86 dt 25.9.86 and Raj Kumar Singh vs The State of Bihar & Ors. W. (Cr. A. 353/86) dt 25 9.86. Judged on the basis of 911 the said principles there is no ground for interference with the order of detention as passed. It, however, appears that after the order was passed and before the actual service of the order, the detenu was taken into custody. From the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenue or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles noted in the aforesaid decision and especially in the cases, in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District magistrate Etah and Ors. , though there was a statement to the effect that the detenu 's release from one prison to another was considered but the need to serve the detention order while he was in custody was not properly considered by the detaining authority in the instant case, in the facts and circumstances of this case, it is nowhere stated that this factor or the question that the impugned detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of his release, was taken in consideration by the Detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service of order. A bald statement is merely an ipso dixit of the officer. If there were cogent materials for thinking that the detenue might be release then these should have been made apparent. Eternal vigilance on the part of the authority charged with both law and order and public order is the price which the democracy in this country extracts from the public officials in order to protect the fundamental freedoms of our citizens.

The respondents were engaged in gold trade, i.e., manufacturers, shroffs and dealers in gold. They carried on business as such dealer. The Administrator issued a notice to the respondents under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for refusing permission or grant permission to carry on business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on the business as a dealer. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court struck down the provisions only on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or granting permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carried on money lending or banking business on a security of article, bullion or both unless authorised by the administrator. The High Court also struck down sec. 28 in the manner done and in its judgment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. The main object in putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " In other words, the several restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. It is also clear that the restrictions which have been imposed in sec.28 are meant to prevent the circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Therefore, in our view the objective, the policy and the Scheme of the impugned Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention by the other provisions is clearly inapplicable. [955E F] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division, while declaring unamended sec. 27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague. For instance under clause (a) the Administrator was also required to have regard to the anticipated demand ' as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression "anticipated demand" was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1)AIR 1971 Patna 240; (2)14 Guj. L.R. 112; and (3)14 Gujarat High Court in Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors. , referred to.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, filed an application before the Magistrate under section 87 of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (XLIII Of 1951) for possession of certain properties. The Magistrate held that the grant was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the appellants, the lower appellate court reversed the finding of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In second appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that (i) the question as to whether on facts proved in the present case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of the temple; and (ii) the transfer made by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment is challenged by his successor on the ground that it is beyond the authority of the manager. HELD : (i)(a) The question whether the facts proved showed not only that the alienor disposed of all the property and left the village but also that for the last 25 years or so, the management has been taken over by other person who are acting as managers of a deity. [132 D] (b) The fact that the properties belonged to the temple had in course of time been a alienated and the alienors were no longer interested either in the temple or in staying in the village itself. Therefore, it was plain that limitation began as soon as the purchaser took possession of the office under article 124. It is true that immovable properties belonging to the endowment had also been sold; but the Privy Council expressly ruled that there was no distinction between the office and the property of the endowment. The one is attached to the other; but if there is, article 144 of the same Schedule is applicable to the property; and that bars the suit after 12 years ' adverse possession. Similarly in Damodar Das 's case, it is substantially because of this decision that Articles 134 A, 134 B and 134 C came to be inserted in the First Schedule to the Limitation Act by Amending Act 1 of 1929. [133 D E] (c) The title of the alienees in regard to the properties covered by the said sale deed was held to have conferred title on them. The appellants ' case before the trial Court was that Pachaikandaswamiar had resigned his position about 27 years ago, and that even if article 134 B applied, limitation should be held to commence from the date when they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 4 on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowments, but on the assumption that the property belonged to them. [134 E F] (d) The appellants had been claiming beneficial interest in the properties all along and that they were not holding the same as managers. Therefore there was a clear distinction between Pachaukandaswami or manager of the Hindu Religious endowment. [135 G] (e) The High Court erred in reversing the decision of the courts below by holding that the title of Pachaakandaswami could not be sustained.

The appellant, who was the sole licensee of a cinema theatre, had applied to the District Magistrate for permission to construct a modern Cinema Hall at the proposed site, a detailed description of which was furnished in the plan annexed to the application. The District Magistrate rejected the request of the appellant and declared that the licence granted by the Government was in favour of the respondent. The State Government preferred an appeal against the order of the District Judge. The High Court upheld the order holding that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that even though the licence had originally been issued in the name of the firm, the right of operation of the licence has become the property of the partnership by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the Partnership Deed and since the said procedure has not been followed by the District Collector, the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order is not one suspending the licence issued in respect of the Theatre. What was done thereunder is to suspend the exhibition of cinematograph films in the Theatre by persons other than the licensee. [581G] 2. On a reading of the provisions contained in the Act and the Rules and the explicit terms of the license itself, it is impossible to sustain the view expressed in the judgment under appeal that the license is a grant for the premises and constitutes an interest attached to the premises. In this case, on a reading, of the provision contained in section 6 F of the Act, and the rules and the specific terms of licence itself, the Court has no hesitation to hold that the view taken by the High Court that the impugned Order was violative Of principles of Natural justice is erroneous. [582C D] 3. The right to conduct the exhibition by grant of licence and the power to administer and enforce the provisions of the statute and the Rule clearly include the power of revocation, embodied in section F of Act and an implied power to suspend a licence pending the proceed ings for such revocation, the District magistrate had no jurisdiction or power to suspended the licence. [583F G] 4. The order passed by the State Government directing the suspension of cinema shows that it was passed by him in the exercise of his function of administering the provision of the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 as one implicit in the larger power of revoke revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the said section are present, the licensing Authority had no Jurisdiction or power under any other circumstances. [584D E] 5.

The respondent, who was the evacuee of a composite character consisting of three distinct matters. There was a lease for five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 10 of the , calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not he evicted. The notice then went on to state that the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises, and the appellants were accordingly required not to remove the stock or raise any money on the security thereof, and to send daily reports to the Custodian. The respondent contended that section 12 applied only to properties of the evacuee and that the movables in respect of which directions were given ceased to be the property of the appellant by reason of the sale in favour of the appellants. Held, that the rights of the parties in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the Mills and the Factory was not raised in the petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The provisions of section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1954, were intended to repel a possible contention that section 10 applied only where there was a contract between the parties and that it was not put forward at any stage prior to the bearing of this appeal and that by itself would be sufficient ground for refusing to entertain it which it may be noted was now sought to be raised by a supplemental proceeding under Order 16, r. 4 of the Supreme Court Rules. The section expressly authorises the custodian to vary the terms of the lease, and that cannot be reconciled with the contention of the respondents that it confers no authority on him to go back upon his own contracts. Held further, that in view of the decision of this Court in Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose (I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant, a minor son of the respondent, filed a writ petition in the High Court for setting aside the order dated 6th August, 1977 passed by the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court on 19th July, 1979 holding that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court had rightly held that there is no provision under section 9 of the Land Revenue Act for separate unit in Chapter Ill B of Rajasthan Tenancy Act (Act 3 of 1955). [728G] 2. Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Ordinance (No.XXII of 1949) provides as under "221. Subordination of revenue courts. The general superintendence, control and control of all revenue Courts shall be vested in, an all such courts shall be subordinate to the Board; and subject to such superintendence, Control and subordination (a) x x (omitted) (b) all Additional Collectors, Sub Divisional Officers, Assistant Collectors and Tehsildars in a district shall be Subordinate to the Collector thereof. " [729B C] 3. The contention on behalf the appellant is that the section confers executive powers of superintendence and Control on the Board and it does not vest any power of superintendence on the board on judicial side.

The expression `newspaper ' is defined by section 2(b) of the Act as any working journalist, and includes any other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. The expression "working journalist" is defined in Section 2(c) of that Act as an establishment under the control of any person or body of persons whether incorporated or not, for the production or publication of one or more newspapers or for conducting any news agency or syndicate. The respondent, a newspaper employee, was employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity and was employed in a supervisory capacity performing either by the nature of the duties attached to his office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature. A non journalist newspaper employee ' means any person employed mainly for recording current events, and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, journals which, in so far as they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets both into one another. The appellant, a non journalist, was not served with any individual notice by the Tribunal before it passed its award. The 1st respondent also did not send a reply to the questionnaire issued by the Central Government on the recommendations of the Justice Palekar Award as the orders of the Central Govern ment made under section 12 of the . The first respondent submitted its written statement in October 1981 inter alia contending that it was not running a newspaper establishment and publications published by the company were not the newspapers and as such the Palehan Award was not applicable to it. The Tribunal accepted the plea of the Ist respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2 (b) and that the demand made by the Deputy Labour Commissioner to comply with the order made by it on the basis of the recommendations made by Justice P.alekar was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The first Respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the 1st respon dent and also the demand for implementation of the Peekar Award. The High Court accepted the contention of the first respondent and held that the public was not interested in them. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by a non newspaper employee within the expression `public news ' is of sufficiently wide amplitude to cover the publications of both the petitioners in question. [782G] 1.2 The term `new ' is usually applied (except so faras concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current event, and 'periodical ' to future events, review their journals and journals. It is well known that the decisions of the superior courts while they settle the disputes between the parties to the proceedings in which they are given them are the sources of law in so much far as all others are concerned. [781C D] 1:3 The word `new" is not defined in the Act.

The appellant, a monthly tenant of the suit premises, filed ejectment proceedings against one 1060 Sugrabhai Mohammed Husain, their tenant and obtained a decree. It was stated that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. Clause 2 of the agreement provided that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The appellant, therefore, filed an ejectment proceeding against the respondent under section 41 of the Bombay City Weavers Cooperative Limited Act, 1948. The trial Judge passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st January, 1975. Before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to respondent for conducting business. It is further contended that there was sub tenancy by the Respondent in favour of the appel lant as a monthly licensee of the business with the articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent. The respondent, therefore filed an application under section 115 C.P.C. in the High court for a fresh decision keeping in view the decision of this Court in D.H. That decision was remanded back to the High COurt for a afresh decision keeping the decision in Errington vs Erringtrington, ; and allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The view taken by the High Courts or the Court of Small Causes is incorrect. It has been a possible view. [1062E] 2.1 In determining whether an agreement creates a lease rather than a licence, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the court had to jurisdiction, and there was no estoppel. [1160F G] 2:2 The background of the entire document negate the contention of the respondent that it was a lease and not a licence. good deal of submission was made before the Court that if it was the lease and was not a license, then the point could he taken in assistance of the submissions that the Court had to Jurisdiction, and that there is no estoppel in favour or the respondent.[1060G] 2 :3 The background and background of this case and the background of entire document nullify the contention. [ 1061F G; 1062A B] 2(a) In determining Whether an agreement created between the parties the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the erstwhile Dholpur state into the Matsya Union. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Bikaner State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently, in June 1947, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni before December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. The respondent filed suits against the State of Rajasthan on various grounds but the suits were resisted by the State on several grounds; but the High Court held that in view of article 295(2) of the Constitution the State was bound by any liability which might have arisen against the former State of Dholpur unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the agreement dated December 2o, 1947, was not a special law and did not fall within article 295 (2) as there was no recognition of the right by the new sovereign. The agreement was not in dispute that on the merger provision was made for the continuance of the laws in the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the old State. The new State had been recognised by the Indian States and it was on January 26, 1950, that there was recognition of liability by the said new State throughout this process and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part B State of Rajgarh in view Of article 295 of the Covenant and similar provisions which were always made throughout this period. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The Union of India, ; , referred to.

The appellants who were running the market as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar was challenged by them on the ground that they contravened article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed their applications holding that section 5(4)(a) of Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, was void to the extent it conferred on the Collector authority to refuse a licence at his own discretion and rule 37 was void in so far as it prohibited persons whose names had not yet been registered as buyers and sellers from carrying on business in the notified area. Held, that the provisions of the Madras Act were valid and did not contravene article 19 (1)(g) of 'the Constitution. Section 14(4) of Act prohibits a person within a notified area from setting up, establishing or using continuing or allowing to be continued more than one place in the same notified area for the purchase, sale, storage, weighment, pressing or processing of any notified commercial crop except under and in accordance with the conditions of a licence granted to him by the Collector. The provisions of section 107 of the Act were not ultra vires article 19 of the constitution as it was bad because the market committee did not name the allowance or allowances taking them out of the pro hibition under section 14 which they were entitled to do under that section, but made the bye law mentioning the mahimai ' allowance as one not deductible in any transaction. The fact that a market is established does not prevent a trader from carrying out the business in a market established, but he could not run a market for himself in respect only of the commodities declared to be commercial crops within the radius prescribed.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions judge. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of imprisonment to transportation for life. Held, that in a case like that the accused all ran away from the scene of occurrence and their Lordships took that into consideration to establish a common intention. There was no evidence of any prior meeting. 1096 In the present case there was no inconsistency between the facts disclosed in the F.I.R. and the FI.L. The fact that the appellants were charged with the murder and the injury on the throat is ascribed to him in the charge. The mere absence of the names in the report is not of much consequence in this case especially as the names were disclosed in full at the time of the inquest. There were three sets of committal proceedings, and of course the usual questioning by the police and then the proceedings in the Sessions Court, so it was not unusual to convict the appellants on that basis. The absence of names in F. I. R. is no evidence to show that they ran away together as a body, or that they met afterwards. There is no inconsistency in this respect. In the absence of anything specific there is no special rule of evidence for this class of case. The present case was not one of fact and therefore the conviction should be altered to one of ten years ' rigorous imprisonment. That apart there was some vague evidence to indicate that they run away together. The medical evidence shows that the injury caused death was the one on the neck.

The petitioner, who was working in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing, was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. He challenged that order before this Court on the ground that he had not attained the age of 50 years by the date of the impugned order. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class 117 he could not have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). [637C D] 1.2 Sub clause (ii) is the general rule applicable to all Government servants and sub clause(i) carves out a class of Govern ment servants into a category and makes a special provision. The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii), has a purpose behind it. If the rule indicated in sub clause.(i) is satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in Class I or class II service or post and he had entered into service before attaining the age Of 35 years, and has attained the quen tion of fifty, the further condition that he must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme. The object of Fundamental Rule 56 (j) is not to confer a right to the post and at any time the Government Servant may be sent back to his substantive post. There is, however, no reasons why sub clause should be confined to service or Post held on substantive basis. [638E F] 1:3 The purpose for Fundamental Rules56(j)(i) was to confer powers on the competent authority to prematurely retire Government servants in the Public interest and classification of Govern m servants into one categories covered under sub clauses(i), (ii). [ 635F G] 2.4 Sub clause(ii) carves Out a class Of Government servants from a category, and makes special provision.[637G H] 5.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. The appellant Corporation contested the suit contending that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It was further stated in the plaint that the office of the Divisional Manager of Masilipatam was concerned authority to settle the claim of the plaintiffs respondents and to pay the amount. The contention of the appellant was that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first premium and therefore it was the case of the plaintiff respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal and the allegation about the assurance given to the deceased as alleged in the pleadings was not true nor the alleged assurance if any valid under law. It is further stated that the averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment of the first premiums would amount to acceptance of proposal and advised the deceased to pay to the first insurance premium in full. The Trial Court held that there were no concluded contracts between the appellant and the respondent Corporation, and that as per the prospectus of Life Insurance Corporation of India the risk under the Corporation policy commenced on the date when receipt of balance towards the premium by it was only consistent with the acceptance of its proposal. It further held that the other averments in this claim that there had been a concluded contract were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance or of the proposals if the proposal was not otherwise accepted. The High Court also took the view that the Corporation has not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case, the Assistant Divisional Manager to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that (1) there was a concluded and valid insurance contract between them and the Life Insurance Corpn. of India; and (2) the plea that Divisional Manager was the only competent authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf of the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the death of the applicant or the mere preparation of the policy document is not acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance. [359D E] 2.

The respondent filed a suit for an interim injunction restraining the appellant in the suit from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.O Tractors Export, Moscow, and the second defendant. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that an order granting interim injunction was final and as such determining the rights of parties within this category or proceeding which is independent though ancillary to the suit, and they were competent to grant the certificate. In appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(a) and (b), HELD: (i) The expression "judgment" in article 133 (1) means a final adjudication on the rights and liabilities of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; if the rights or obligations of the party in dispute are not a judgment, however cardinal the issue may be. In the present case not even an issue has been decided and it is not contended that the order of the High Court amounts to a judgment or "a decree". The expression 'final order ' occurring in article133 (1)(b) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. [707 G] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, ; , applied. (ii) In the instant case not only an issue had been decided but it was not contended by the respondent that the High court has departed from the principle of the earlier decisions or has suggested a different test for determining the finality of orders. [700 G H] Ram Chand Manjimal V. Goverdadas Vishind as Ratan Chand vs Kesho Prasad Singh, A.I.R. 1958 S.C.R 1007, applied.

The petitioners, who were engaged in processing of processed fabric, filed a writ petition before the High Court contending that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value and manufacturing expenses. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the price at which he was selling the processed goods in the market would include only the price or deemed price at what the processed fabrics would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price on which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabil ities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at Which he is selling his goods must be the price of the grey cloth or fabric plus the values of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. [346C D] 2. Rule 173 enjoins that whenever goods owned in by one persons are manufactured, by another, the information was required relating t to the prices at which the aforesaid manufacturer is sell ing the saidgoods and the persons so authorised agree to discharge All the liablities under this Act and rules made thereof. The prices at Which the processed cloth would leave, the processor"s factory minus his profit [346D] 3. Rule 172 enjoins that where goods owned are manufactured in one person, the fact is required relates to the value at which they have sold the processed product, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [347E F] 4.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975, he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The appellant was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974, he filed a writ petition in the High Court asking that he should be absorbed as a head clerk. The writ petition having been dismissed by the High court, the appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant is entitled to be considered for promotion to the post on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the respondent Panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section 14(4) of the Amending Act, the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though, as stated earlier, he is working as aHead Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [737E G] 1.2 The appointment of the petitioner to the posts of Head Clerks being without the authority of law, the government was not bound to absorb him in the post or of a Head clerk. He was appointed lawfully to the Post of a Clerk and that was the post which the respondent No.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math, and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati had not been a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saauna and Sarbakar of deity. Two appeals were filed in the High Court. First Appeal No. 80 of 1964 was filed by Kedar Nath Choudhury @ Uma Shankar Yadav, against the declaration that the Amauli properties were owned by Mahant Shivshankar Yati and that Sadasiv Yatati was not a regularly appointed Mahant of the Math and that the son of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yutti had inherited the property as Mahant. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the properties had been purchased by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yatti in 1921 from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivpher Yati, and the Amaul properties must, therefore, be regarded as his personal property and separate properties and they did not belong to the math or deity. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum and must, consequently, be treated as property belonging to the Mahant and must be regarded in his personal and independent properties and that they did no belong to Math or the deity; and that when a nuchacleus was dedicated property there could be no presumption either way. All the facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to Mahant or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. In the present case it was difficult to conclude from the material before this Court that the total income from the properties belonging to Math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh who was 42 330 found entitled to quasi permanent allotments of 40 standard acres, and 5 1/4 unit of land was given quasipermanent allotment in another village named Humbran in the same district. The two villages were, however, 25 miles or so distant from each other. Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the Village Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. This application was rejected on the ground that no land was available in the villages Raikot and that consequently their allotment had been wrongly made but referred the matter back to the Additional Custodian for decision. The Additional Custodian held that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban lands at all. On appeal by the appellant, the Deputy Custodian General set aside the order cancelling the allotment of land in favour of the appellant on the grounds (1) that the notification issued thereunder stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour Of the appellants and (2) that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in that way. Held, that the power conferred by section 19(1) of , is to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. The power of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour to a displaced person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. But the consequence of the publication of the notification by the Central Government under section 12(1), with respect to any property or a class of property would be to divest the Custodian completely of his right in the property flowing from section 8 of the , and vest that property in the Central Govern ment. He would, therefore, not be competent to deal with the property in any manner in the absence of any provision in either of these two enactments permitting him to do so.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women 's Branch) in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women). The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the Written examination were selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Commis sion decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that the candidate had better perform in the oral examina tions were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the interview from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina ion. On the other hand, it is contended on their behalf that when there was a defect pointed out, there could be no justification to cancel them and asking for a re opening of the written test and select those who on the bases of the Written exami ne were not even called for interviews but were finally selected; that when this position had been known and on an inquiry it was factually established, the public Service Commission decided to cancellation the entire selection examination and directed the State Public Service Depart ment to re hold the recruitment examination. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. Som Dass, the defendant contended that the Dhoh at Landake was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of those properties as its lawfully appointed mahant, that the appellant had no right to recover possession of that property of the dhoh and entitled to manage the properties of the Dharera, and that the plaintiff was not entitled to any possession of it. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass he as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. On appeal by special leave: HELD: (1) The devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit took place when Shiam Dass was elected as mahant of the Palera after the demise of Som Das. Som Das was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of the Rhoh, he was its lawfully appoint mahant and that he had no rights to recover any possession thereof. [489E F] (2) The suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacities as de facto mahant. In other words, the suit was for possession and management of the Phoh by virtue of his election as matithant subsequent to the death. [490F G] (3) The appeal could be continued under Q. 22 r. 10 notwithstanding the fact that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired.

The petitioners who were working as ministerial or non ministerial but not belonging to the last grade service, who had already attained the age of 55 years was to retire from service with effect from February 28, 1983. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification on October 29, 1979 stating that it had decided to reduce the age for superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 to 58 years. Two notifications were issued in exercise of the power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution and the petitioners challenged the said order and the notifications on the ground that they violate Articles 14, 16, 21 and 300A of the constitution. The case of the petitioners was that there was no basis at all for reducing the age retirement from 58 and that the age was increased from 55 to 58 by the Government of India by a notification dated October 29. 1979 and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age from 55 years. The State Government, however, rejected their contention on the view that it was arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it sought to achieve. In the writ petitions filed before this Court, the petitioners contended that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the State exchequer would have to find and pay Rs. 70 crores on one single day by way of retirement benefits, for which no budgetary provision was made; that as a result of the increase in the age, the chances of promotion of the service personnel had deteriorated resulting in widespread frustration and unemployment; that it would have resulted in grave detriment to public services of the State; and that, the decision to reduce their age of retirement from 55 was arbitrary and irrational and hence violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned action of the Government is bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the date of the report to justify a departure from it. [610 D] 2. The power conferred under H 610 the proviso to Article 311 read with article 313 is of a legislative character and is to be distinguished from an ordinary rule making power. Therefore, the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of power conferred on Hates by the proviso cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amend retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had accrued to them. [613 E] 3. The amendment made in February, 1983 to the Rules was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. No. The contention that the amendment to the Rule was beyond its powers could not be accepted because it is unscientific and unconnected With the object sought to achieved. [514 F G] 4. The fact that the decision in Moti Ram Deka had no application to the case before them since "that case did not deal with any rule relating to age of superannuation" was taken by her State Government within one month of the assumption of office by it cannot justify the conclusion that lt the decision is arbitrary because it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement age at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [625 G H] 5.

The appellants, a registered dealer in the State of Haryana, purchased raw materials inside the State without paying tax thereon. He then sold the manufactured goods to dealers who, in turn exported those goods out of India. On these facts it was claimed that the assessee was not liable to pay purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. This claim was rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. The appellants contended that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. It was further contended that section 9 (1) exempts only sales made in the course of export within the meaning of section 5(1). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act" and "the purchase value of any goods on the sales of which tax is levied under this . [353F] 2. The term "dis poses of" in section 9 of the C.S.T. Act, does not include the words 'disposes or despatches the manufactured ' goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the con tention of section 9. [353G] 3. The word "export" is defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the 361 State to any place outside it otherwise than through way of inter state trade or commerce". There can be no dispute that a tax is payable under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them. [352F G] 4. The words "or despatches" used therein cannot be read ejusdem generis with the word 'dis posing '.

The appellants who were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton sold by them to their sellers on the ground that these sales were oil FOB contracts and they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption but assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including those sales. He also assessed them as to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Act. On appeal by the sellers, the High Court held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till they had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). Held, that the words " a person " in section 8(b), must be interpreted to include a registered dealer or anybody else. The intention of the parties was that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of Imports (Control) Order, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the time of export would therefore mean nothing more than that the property in the goods should pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial waters of the country or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. The words " person " used in section 10 (b) must be construed to include the registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The scheme of the Legislature clearly was that where the intention as declared has not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. To hold otherwise would be to make the declaration of the intention useless.

The appellant married the respondent 's wife. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance, it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she has now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The appellant 's contention was that there must be proof of neglect to maintain attract section 125 and his third contention was based on contractual arrangement in the consent decree read with section 127(3)(b) which reads: "C "(b) the woman has been divorced by her husband and that she had received, whether before or after the date of the said order, the whole of the sum which under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties, was payable on such divorce cancel such order, (i) in the case where such sum was paid before such order from the date on which such order was made. (ii) in any other case from the dates of expiry of the period, if any, for which maintenance has been actually paid by the husband to the woman; and (iii) in a case from a date of expiry, if no claim for maintenance could survive. The trial court held that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. On appeal, the Sessions Judge held that there was no specific plea based on the latter provision set up anywhere in the courts below or urged before this Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case, on the contrary, is that she forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decrees. Obviously, he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect of maintenance is satisfied. [78 E F] 1.2 The appellant had not examined herself to prove his case on the basis of a settlement by which she was a divorcee. Her plea is her right to deny. So, the basic conditions of neglect must easily fail. The consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available But here is a new statutory right created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962, they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. No settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee under section 125 can operate to negate that claim. Nor can s.127 rescue the respondent from his obligation. Payment of mehar money, as a customary discharge, is within the cognisance of that provision. But what was the amount of mehahar ? Rs. 5000/ , interest from which could cannot keep the woman 's body and soul together for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul ? The point must be clearly under stood that the scheme of the complex of provisions in Chapter IX has a social purpose. Ill used wives and desparate divorcees shall not be driven to material and moral dereliction to seek sanctuary in the streets. This traumatic horror animates the amplitude of section 127 and the benefit of doubt. If any in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill used wife and the derelict divorcee, this social perspective granted, the resolution of all the disputes projected is easy. Surely, Parliament, in keeping with article 15(3) and deliberate by design, made a special provision to help women in distress cast away by divorce.

The appellant, who was the successful bidder for a shop in an auction held on 27.3.88, had secured a sum of Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an open auction of his house. The name of the appellant was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector. The letter dated 25th March, 1988 stated that the Collector after perusal of the said office note passed order on 25.3,88 which is produced in verbatim below: "The Collector of the district after perusal, passed an order on the 25.03.1988 which is produce in verb below: Ist bidder chunki defaulter atah security prapt kar len tatha bhavishya ke liae Black list karen. " Indisputably, no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the contention that there is no requirement specifically of giving an opportunity is concerned, the respondent is right. But it is an implied principle of the rule that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. It has to be realised that black listing a person in respect of business ventures has civil consequences for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is not an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In this view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far to which it directs black listing of the petitioner in respect thereof cannot be sustained in law.
