The petitioner, who was a respondent in the writ petition, filed an application before the High Court for a direction to the Union of India to file his objections against the preliminary list. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the case now before it was governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the Act must be given an opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. As already observed above, the petitioner had ample opportunity to do that. Hence, the principle recognised in Shankriah ' s case was not applicable to such a case. [829E F] 2. The combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [828F G] 3. A right to representation was recognised as existing at time when the list was still to be considered as not finalised presumably because some mistakes had crept in due to want of heating on two points. The petitioner had adequate opportunity to make a representation against the final gradation lists. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority list.[828F] 4. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous considerations ation, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [829G H; 829A B] 5. The Central Government had acted properly in accordance with the provisions of the . It was also held there (at p. 2106): "It is no doubt true that the Central Govern ment must have due regard to the princi ples enunciated by it in consultation with the States for the purpose of equation of posts and preparation of gradation lists." [828C D] 6. The respondents were entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to two points urged by the petitioner before the final list was to be declared and published as a final list.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the conditions was that the Additional licences issued to Export House would also be valid for the import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and 5 Part A and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by Appendix 1 Part A) and items available under this Policy. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant or renewal of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that they had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court which allowed the same and directed the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import Policy 1978 79 within three months. While giving the said direction, the High Court imposed a condition in 237 the same terms as laid down by this Court in its order dated April 18, 1985, referred to above. The writ petitions and the appeal were decided by the Bombay high Court in accordance of the decision of this Court In the case of Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, ; and the High Courts directed the Authorities to grant export House Certificates for the year 1978 79. While doing so, this Court observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for the grant or entitlement of an Export House certificate in theImport Policy for 1981 79 and the Export Houses who were issued Additional Licences prior to April 1, 1988, on the basis of their exports during that period subsequent to 1986 87. The High Court further directed the respondents to issue necessary Export Certificates for year 197879 within three month. While disposing of the writ petitions, this court observed that the grantees of the Additional Licences was not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy 1978 80 but also from importing item excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that the word "banned" was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are `canalised ' could not be ruled out and it was in this light that the Court can be said to have used the words "whether canalised or otherwise ' contained in the order dated 4th April, 1988. The matter was further clarified by this court in D. Navinchandra & Co. Bombay & Anr. vs Union of lndia, ; wherein this Court had observed that it would not know whether in the future certain canalised items could be imported directly by an Export house holding an Additional licence and that possibility of a policy being framed in the past enabling an Export Houses holding an additional licence to directly import items which is `non canalised ' and also item which are 'canalised" could not he ruled out.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at Visakhapatnam. It manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture, it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the aforesaid drums were sup plied by the customers for the purpose of filling the fusel oils/Stirene M accessioner. No duty of excise, therefore could be collected from the appellant on such drums which were nei ther manufactured nor purchased by the appellant. The said drums were supplied by the buyer to the customer at the appellant 's factory. The appellant had filed its price lists in respect of the same. In the said price lists, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector, the appellant had shown the value of fusel gas/Slyrene Moulders manufactured according to the appel lant at the rate at which those were sold in wholesale as "naked Ex Works and in bulk". According to the appellant, the manufacture of fuel oil is complete and it is the fully manufactured fusel on behalf of the appe lant. It was also the contention that on a correct and true interpretation of Section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the cost of packing could be included in the assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by him. The Assistant Collector included the value in the price lists. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included In the assessable Value. The Tribunal, therefore, accepted the revenue 's contention and restored the order of the Asstt Collector. Collector. Aggrieved therefrom, the appell lant has come up in these appeals to this Court. On behalf of appellant it was contended that the Tribunal had failed to appreciate the admitted factual position that the fu Counsel oil/styreneMonomer manufactured by it is sold in bulk and is capable of being so sold. Hence according to him, it was not necessary for the said company to be supplied to the customers in drums in the aforesaid situation. The respondent State contended that in any event under the Act and the Rules, the duty of Excise is payable by the manufacturer on the manufactured goods. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to be deliverable, it has to be borne in mind that the duty is chargeable with reference to the value charged by the manufacturers, the computation being made in accordance with the terms of section 4. It has also to be bear in mind the fact that the measure of excise duty is price and not value.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the appellant, who thereupon arranged a trap. As instructed, PW 1 was ready with ten rupees currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant and handed over the money to the appel lant who received the same. When PW 1 emerged, PW 6 along with PW 2 confronted the appellant. The appellant produced the currency notes and PW 6 conducting the phenoolph thalein tests with reference thereto to the finger of the appeLant. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. At the trial, the prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10 .1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The Trial Court accepted the plea of the accused and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the complainant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appe lant was probable and there is no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appella nt. was guilty. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [337F] (2) The High Court thought that though the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. [336G H] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; C.I.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport. On May 21, 1974 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement i.e. for six months after his retired from service. The company on humanitarian grounds acceded to this request and permitted the petitioner to stay on the company "s flat for six month after his retire ment and in accordance with the company"s rules, he was required to pay compensation for the use of the premises. After the expiry of the said period of six months, the company addressed a letters requesting the Company to permit the petitioner company to continue in the Company 's flat during the aforesaid period. The Company on humanitarian ground acceded to it and permitted him to stay in the appellant 's house during the said periods. On March 3, 1986 he addressed another letter asking the Company not to allow him to live therein during the above period. Since the petitioner failed to vacate the flat, the Company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act 1971. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the Single Judge following the earlier decisions of the High Courts in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Ranjan Jha & Anr., [1987] Supp. SCC 634 and Govind T. Jagtiani vs Sirajuddin, ; , held that it refers only to the existing officers and employees of a company and not to those whose employment has been terminated. The Division Bench also held that the words "any such property" in section 630(l)(b) relate to property specified in cl. (a) viz., property of a Company wrongfully taken possession of by a present officer or employee of the company. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court of Calcutta in Amrit Lal Chum 's case obviously fell into an error in seeking to curtail the ambit of section 630 (l)(a) by giving a restrictive meaning to the terms "officer or employee" which must take its colour from the context in which it appears. [179E F] 1:2 The whole object of enacting sub section (1) of section 629 is the preservation of the property of the Company by the creation of two distinct offences by clauses (a), (b) and (c) which arise under different sets of circumstances, and it would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl.(a) into cl. There is also no warrant for the construction placed by the High court of Calcutta on the words 'any such thing ' occurring in cl.(b) as applicable to such property of any company, possession of which is wrongfully obtained by an officer or employees of the companies during his employment, wrongfully retains or occupies the same after the termination of his employment.

The appellant was the founder of a private temple. The deity installed in the temple was a public religious endowment and it had immovable properties of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950, an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons who were members of the public. The Assistant Charity Commissioner held that the Sansthan was not a public trust and ordered its registration as a public Trust under the Act. On appeal, the District Judge reversed the decision of the Assistant Charity Officer and declared the Sansthan to be a private property and not a Public Trust. In an application made by three of the persons representing the Sansthan evidence of the attorney, the High Court held that it was a private religious endowment. The High Court also relied on an admission of the appellant 's witness, Ramkrishna Deshpande, when he stated that "we cannot prevent people from going to the temple as the temple is meant for Darshan by the public". Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. [521 D] (2) The appellant relied on all these documents for the purpose of showing that the endowment was a Public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and section 2 (17) respectively of the .

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 52 by the Third Income tax Officer, C. 1st Ward, Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said demand. The Additional Collector attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the premises by a warrant issued on the 24th March 1954. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March 1955. The sales were held on 25th January 1955 fetating a price which was confirmed by the Additional Collector on the 7th June, 1955 issued a notice under section13 of the Act requiring the appellant to appear in person before him on the 15th January, 1955 and to show cause as why he, should not he apprehended and confine to civil prison in satisfaction Of the said certified demand. No payment having been made, the Additional collector attached the good goodwill and the tenancy rights of the assessee by a warrants of attachment issued on 24th April 1954. On the 16st June 1955 an Advocate acting on behalf of the appellant wrote a letter to the Additional District Collector purporting to showcause why he be not apprehended and should not confined to Civil jail in the satisfaction of his certified demand, and the sale proceeds not being sufficient to satisfy the assessed tax the Additional Collecter attached the assets prior to the amendment. The High Court discharged the rule. No application was made to the High Court for leave to appeal to this Court from the decision of that High Court but on the 2nd September 1955 a rule was issued by which a petition under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity or otherwise of section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was filed in this Court under article 226 of the Constitu tion. Held: (i) The proviso does not indicate a different and alternative mode of recovery of the certified amount of arrears due but only confers additional powers on the Collector for the better and more effective application of the only mode of recovering the amount due under a decree. The other way in which the protection of article 14 is invoked is founded on a comparison of the provisions of the different laws adopted by different States for the recovery of land revenue. Section 46(1) of Bombay City Act, 1879, which authorises the Collectors in different states to adopt the procedure prescribed by their own State laws as if the provisions prescribing that procedure were set out in that section. In such a situation it is a plausible argument to say that all the provisions Of all the State laws for recovery of arrears of land Revenue have been referentially incorporated in section 46 (2) and that, therefore, if there be any vice of discrimination in the State law that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section 46.(2). The two sections operate together and they are not severable. The two provisions operate together. They operate together, though the same are distinct and separate. In order to hold that all these provisions operate equally, it is necessary that the Collector should have recourse to the machinery available to him for enforcing a demand for arrears of Land Revenue, he must have recourse under the machinery provided by his own State law as if he were an arrear of land tax.

The respondents, who were the trustees of the Port Trust Employees ' Union, made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours. The Trustees alleged that this was a device to get 4 hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. The General Workers Union was informed that if the demand was pressed a three shift system would be introduced. The workmen then retraced their steps and accepted a 2 hours ' variable recess but requested that it should be as near the middle of the shift as possible. The respondents refused to accept the demands. The Union contended that this division of 12 hours ' shift into 8 hours ' work, 2 hours and 4 hours was inclusive of one or more specified intervals. Held, that the provisions of section 13 (2) (c) read with section 13(3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest. If it is the latter, it is counted as actual work period: if the former, it was counted as a period of rest provided the period is specified beforehand, and the workman is neither called upon to work nor expected to work. Having thus distinguished between period of work and intervals of rest in sub rules (1) and (2), of Rule 24 and the phrase 'inclusive of one Or more specified interval ' governs the normal working day and not the number of hours of work. Under sub rule (2)(c) of Rule 25, the working day of an adult can be so arranged that inclusive of intervals of all rest it does not exceed 12 hours on any day.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the premises were let out to him by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976. The suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that in view of the language of Section 2 sub clause (2) Explanation 1, it could not he doubted that period of 10 years will commence from 160 the date of assessment i.e. October 1. 1976 and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act would not be available to the tenant. The High Court set aside the decree holding that if the suit was instituted within a period of exemption then the suit should be decreed and the provisions of the Act will not be applicable. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that in the decision in Suraj Prakash Gupta 's case this Court took the view that if during the pendency of the proceedings 10 years have elapsed the tenant is entitled to the benefit of the provisions under Section 20 and that if on the date on which the suit is filed by the respondent the provisions would come to the assistance of the tenants appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under Section 2 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 under Section 19 and the language thereof is also significant. Bar of suit for ejectment of a tenant except on specified grounds (1) Save as provided in sub section (2), no suit shall be instituted for the eviction of a tenants from a building to which the old Act did not apply, pending on the day of commencement of this Act, where the tenant within one month from such date of commencement or from the date when his knowledge of the pendency o.e., whichever be later, deposits in the court before which the suits is pending, the entire amount of rent and damages for use and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlord 's full cost of the suit, no decree for eviction shall be passed except on any of the grounds mentioned in the proviso to sub section(1) or in clauses (b A) to (g) of sub section 2 of Section 20, and the parties shall be entitled to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and adduce additional evidence where necessary. [164D E] Om Prakash Gupta etc. vs Digpal Gupta etc., ; , referred to. In the instant case, the suit itself was filed much after the coming into force of this U. P. The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of the appellant from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1, Shibtola Lane, Entally Calcutta) on the ground that the same were in arrears and that the tenancy right therein was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of a thika tenant in that Act was not similar to section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the landlord that (i) the appellant could not be regarded as a thikika tenant inter alia on the view that with the omission of section 29 civil courts became unable to remit ejectment suits to the controller with the result that the Act as finally amended could not apply to pre legislation suits and thika tenants could get no relief under the Act; (ii) the only power vested in civil courts in respect of ejectment suits against 173 thika tenancy like the present one was to be found in sections 28 and 29 of the original Act and by their omission from the statute "suits for eviction became infructuous before civil courts". HELD: (i)(a) The appellant could have no grievance against the view taken by the High court. [176 D] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. (b) Section 28 was meant to give relief to a th kika tenant if he could establish that he was holding land under any of the systems expressly mention ed or any other like system. The incidents of thika tenancies were mentioned in various sections from section 3 to section II contained in Chapter 11 of the Calcutta Thika Tenant Act, 1949. Section 29 was meant only those persons who inherited from tenants and not those who acquired by purchase.

The appellants were working as Section Officers in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs,120 300 to Section Officers. In 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers and Rs. 150 500 1,000. The Government accepted the recommendations. Subsequently, these pay scales were raised to Rs. 200 450 and Rs 15 715 respectively. Being dissatisfied with the down grading, the Bench Secretaries made representation to the Government. They demanded that they should be put at par with Section Officers if not on higher scale. The High Court upheld their claim but half heartedly. Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, the appellants have come up in appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section officers in view of their differential duties. It was found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two posts cannot be said to be equal. Keeping in view the fact that vacancies in Upper Division/Lower Division Assistants are filled up by promotion from Routine Grade Assistants, it is clear that this is a second promotion for those who come directly from Lower Division Assistants and a third promotion for these who come either directly from lower division Assistants and as then a Bench Secretary. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [298G H] 1.2 In comparison to Bench Secretaries, the Section Officers perform onerous duties and bear greater responsibilities than Bench Secretaries. The Court Secretaries Grade I are in a higher pay scale than Bench Secretary Grade II. It is true that at one time, Bench Secretaries were paid more emoluments than Section Officers but it is not known on what basis they were paid in the higher pay scales and treated as a superior class to Section officers. The Commissions and Committee have evaluated the respective duties and responsibility of the posts. It has evaluated the various duties and functions of the three posts. [297B C] 1:3 The Pay Commis sioner cannot be given the same scale of pay which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officer. Since the Bench Judges are promoted from Upper Division Assistants, they should feel satisfied if they are placed in a scale of Pay a little above the Upper Division Secretaries Grade. Therefore, it has recommended for their pay scales admissible to Section Officer with effect from October 1, 1975. [299C D] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the , and the entire share capital being owned by it, the Government of India. The respondent 1, the Special Area Development Authority for the Korba Special Area, was constituted under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam (23 of 1973). Section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 empowers a municipal council to impose, in the whole or any part of the municipality, "a tax payable by the owners of houses, buildings or lands situated within the limits of Municipality with reference to annual letting value of the house, building or land called property tax". The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent Company under which the Company agreed to contribute a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs annually to the "seed capital" of the Authority in consideration of the authority agreeing not to exercise its power of taxation or of levying any other charges on the assets and activities of the Company under the Act. The appellant Company disputed its liability to pay the aforesaid amounts on the grounds, inter alia, that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the Government and that respondent 1 was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The first contention of the Attorney General was that respondent I could exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Corporation or the Municipal Council had under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1956, or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act 1961, as these Acts stood on 12 February 27, 1976, when clause (d) was inserted in its present form in section 69 of the . It was further contended that since the appellant companies were wholly owned by the government of India, the lands 16 and buildings owned by them cannot be subjected to property tax. The companies which are incorporated under Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 or the M.P. Municipalities Act. 1961, have a corporate personality of their own, distinct from that of the Government. On the question as to whether the appellant company carried on an industry under the authority of the Central Government within the meaning of section 2(a) of Madhya Pradesh Panchayat Raj Adhiniyam, 1973, or Madhya Pradesh Panchayats Act, 1961, it was held by this Court that an incorporated Company has a separate existence and the law recognises it as a juristic person, separate and distinct from its members. If the lands and building on which respondent 1 had imposed the property taxes cannot be regarded as the property of the State Government for several other purposes like attachment and sale, there is no reason why, for taxing purposes, the property can be treated as belonging to that Government as distinct from the company which has a juristic personality. The Attorney General also contended that if at all the lands could be subjected by property tax, it is the State Govern ment and not the appellant Companies who can be called upon to pay that tax. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power conferred by the State Legislature on Special Area development Authorities to impose the property Tax on lands and buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred under the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [8C D] 1.2 The power of the state Legislature on special Area Development Authorities to levy the propertytax on lands or buildings is, therefore, not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69(D) of tho Act of 1974.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in his estate for five years. On January 10, 1942, an agreement was entered into between the Rajah of Venkatagiri and one Sri Balumuri Nageswara Rao whereby the Raja agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate quarry within his estate. The lease was for twenty years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947 the said Sri Balamuri Negeswara Rao granted a lease for twenty five years to the appellant. On September 7, 1949, the Raja granted another lease to the said Balumuru Nageswara rao for a short period commencing from January 1, 1948 and ending with November 30. On the expiry of the fifth year, however, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease grant made by the Raja to him. The Collector rejected the application on the ground that it did not satisfy the said authorities. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease granted to the Raja was valid and that as the lease was a period exceeding one year, it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal by the appellant, Held, that the notice dated 13th March 1951, fell under the second Proviso and was valid. The notice dated December 13, 1955, falls under the third proviso and is valid. It is not necessary for the Government to have recourse to the provisions of section 20 of the Act to justify its action on the basis that it does not comply with the conditions laid down in the third provisos.
